marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q001.takeaway: Clavicle is the first bone to begin ossification in embryonic development.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q001.displayText: The clavicle is the first bone to ossify in the human body. It begins ossification in the 5th-6th weeks of intrauterine life. The clavicle is a blend of condensed mesenchyme in the early embryonic phase. At its terminal ends, early cartilage transformation (pre-cartilage) takes place; intramembranous centres of ossification appear and fuse in the mesenchyme between them. Hence, the clavicle ossifies partly in membrane and partly in cartilage.

rationales.a: Humerus begins ossification after clavicle; it is not the first bone to ossify.
rationales.c: Scapula ossifies later and is not the first bone.
rationales.d: Lunate is a carpal bone and ossifies postnatally, not first embryonic bone.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q002.takeaway: Common clavicle fracture occurs near medial 3/5–lateral 2/5 junction, not the fractions stated in option D.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q002.displayText: Fractures of the clavicle typically occur at the junction of the medial 3/5th and lateral 2/5th. The middle-third or midshaft region is the commonest fracture site, especially at this junction. It is the junction where the two primary ossification centres meet and also the transition from a more curved medial segment to a flatter lateral segment, making it a high-risk site. The proximal fragment is displaced upward by sternocleidomastoid and the distal fragment downward by pectoralis major and gravity.
emphasis: junction of the medial 3/5th and lateral 2/5th

rationales.a: Clavicle has both intramembranous and endochondral ossification components.
rationales.b: Clavicle transmits upper-limb load to axial skeleton through coracoclavicular and costoclavicular ligaments.
rationales.c: Clavicle is subcutaneous along its length, making it palpable. The fracture junction is medial 3/5 and lateral 2/5, so option D’s fractions are false.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q004.takeaway: Long head of triceps originates from infraglenoid tubercle, not coracoid.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q004.displayText: In a patient with a coracoid fracture, the action of the long head of triceps muscle is not hindered. The long head of triceps attaches to the infraglenoid tubercle on the lateral border of the scapula, not to the coracoid process. Coracoid process attachments include the origins of coracobrachialis and short head of biceps, insertion of pectoralis minor, and the coracoacromial, coracoclavicular and coracohumeral ligaments.

rationales.a: Coracobrachialis originates from coracoid and is affected by coracoid fracture.
rationales.b: Short head of biceps originates from coracoid and may be impaired.
rationales.c: Pectoralis minor inserts on coracoid and can be affected; long head of triceps attaches at infraglenoid tubercle.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q005.takeaway: Subscapularis inserts on lesser tubercle and can avulse it.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q005.displayText: Forceful contraction of the subscapularis can cause an isolated avulsion fracture of the lesser tubercle of the humerus because subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle. Forceful contraction while resisting abduction and external rotation can avulse this insertion. The other rotator-cuff insertions shown are supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor on the greater tubercle.
emphasis: avulsion fracture of the lesser tubercle

rationales.a: Teres minor inserts on greater tubercle, not lesser tubercle.
rationales.d: Infraspinatus also inserts on greater tubercle; subscapularis attaches to lesser tubercle.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q006.takeaway: Latissimus dorsi attaches to floor of intertubercular sulcus.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q006.displayText: The structure marked A is the intertubercular sulcus (bicipital groove), and latissimus dorsi is attached to its floor. The intertubercular sulcus lies between the greater and lesser tubercles. Attachments around it are: lateral lip - pectoralis major; medial lip - teres major; floor - latissimus dorsi. Contents include the long head of biceps and the ascending branch of the anterior circumflex humeral artery. The source memory tip is 'Lady between two majors': latissimus dorsi lies between pectoralis major laterally and teres major medially.

rationales.b: Teres major attaches to medial lip of intertubercular sulcus, not its floor.
rationales.c: Long head of biceps tendon passes within sulcus but does not insert on its floor.
rationales.d: Pectoralis major attaches to lateral lip; latissimus dorsi inserts into floor.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q007.takeaway: Sternoclavicular joint is saddle-type synovial joint, not hinge.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q007.displayText: The sternoclavicular joint is a synovial saddle joint, not a hinge joint. It is the only skeletal articulation between the upper limb and the axial skeleton.

rationales.a: Acromioclavicular joint is a plane synovial joint, correctly matched.
rationales.d: Intercarpal and midcarpal joints are plane synovial joints; sternoclavicular is saddle rather than hinge.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q008.takeaway: Glenohumeral joint’s high mobility comes at the expense of stability.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q008.displayText: As mobility increases, stability is lost in a joint. The glenohumeral joint is the most mobile joint in the body and is very unstable. It is the most frequently dislocated joint. Shoulder dislocation is more common in adults and is rare in children. Anterior dislocation is much more common than posterior dislocation.

rationales.a: Glenohumeral joint is indeed the most frequently dislocated joint; high mobility contributes to instability.
rationales.c: Shoulder dislocation is less common in children; source states this correctly.
rationales.d: Anterior dislocation is much more common than posterior; option B alone reverses the mobility-stability relationship.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q009.takeaway: Teres major is not a static stabilizer of glenohumeral joint.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q009.displayText: Teres major has no role in maintaining stability of the shoulder joint. Because the humeral head is larger than the glenoid cavity, the shoulder is predisposed to displacement. Stability is provided by the rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis), the tendon of the long head of biceps, and the coracoacromial ligament. Degeneration or tear of these structures leads to instability. The shoulder joint is least protected inferiorly; the capsule is loose and only the long head of triceps crosses the joint inferiorly.

rationales.b: Supraspinatus is a rotator-cuff muscle and contributes to joint stabilization.
rationales.c: Long-head biceps tendon helps stabilize humeral head.
rationales.d: Coracoacromial arch limits superior displacement; teres major is not a joint stabilizer.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q010.takeaway: Pectoralis minor acts on scapula and thorax, not shoulder joint.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q010.displayText: Pectoralis minor has no action at the shoulder joint. It originates from the 3rd-5th ribs near their costochondral junctions and inserts on the medial border and upper surface of the coracoid process. It is an accessory muscle of inspiration and stabilizes the scapula by pulling it anteriorly and inferiorly. The source provides a movement table for the shoulder joint.
emphasis: no action at the shoulder joint

rationales.a: Teres major acts at shoulder joint (adduction, extension, medial rotation).
rationales.c: Subscapularis is a rotator-cuff muscle acting at shoulder and stabilizing it.
rationales.d: Deltoid is a primary shoulder abductor; pectoralis minor does not act on shoulder joint.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q011.takeaway: Lateral humeral rotation increases shoulder abduction by clearing greater tubercle.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q011.displayText: Lateral rotation of the humerus increases the range of abduction. During abduction without rotation, the greater tubercle comes in contact with the coracoacromial arch and prevents further abduction. With lateral rotation toward 180 degrees, the tubercles rotate posteriorly and the more articular surface continues to elevate, increasing the range of abduction.

rationales.a: Adduction is not the range increased; lateral rotation enables further abduction.
rationales.c: Flexion is not the movement facilitated by clearing greater tubercle from coracoacromial arch.
rationales.d: Extension is not increased; the source mechanism specifically permits greater abduction.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q012.takeaway: Scapulohumeral rhythm gives 2 degrees GH motion per 1 degree scapular rotation.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q012.displayText: A normal scapulohumeral rhythm is 2:1. Scapulohumeral rhythm is the ratio of glenohumeral movement to scapulothoracic movement during arm elevation. For example, during 90 degrees of abduction, glenohumeral elevation is about 60 degrees and scapulothoracic rotation about 30 degrees.

rationales.a: 1:1 would overstate scapular rotation relative to glenohumeral elevation.
rationales.d: 3:1 overstates glenohumeral motion; normal GH:scapulothoracic rhythm is 2:1.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q013.takeaway: Long head of biceps tendon runs intracapsularly within shoulder joint.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q013.displayText: The long head of biceps is intracapsular. The fibrous capsule of the shoulder attaches medially to the glenoid neck at a variable distance from the glenoid labrum. The capsule includes the supraglenoid tubercle, to which the long head of biceps attaches, so the long-head tendon lies within the capsule.

rationales.a: Short head of biceps originates at coracoid and is extracapsular.
rationales.b: Medial head of triceps originates on humerus and does not pass through capsule.
rationales.c: Long head of triceps originates from infraglenoid tubercle outside shoulder capsule; long-head biceps is intracapsular.

marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q014.takeaway: Rotator interval lies between supraspinatus and subscapularis.
marrow__ANAT_CH35_Q014.displayText: The rotator interval is the area between supraspinatus and subscapularis. It is a medially based triangular area not covered by capsule. It lies between the superior edge of subscapularis and the anterior edge of supraspinatus, with the coracoid as the medial boundary of the interval. It is reinforced by the coracohumeral ligament, superior glenohumeral ligament, and fibres from the supraspinatus tendon laterally.

rationales.b: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus border other parts of cuff, but interval is between supraspinatus and subscapularis.
rationales.c: Infraspinatus and teres minor are posterior cuff muscles, not rotator-interval margins.
rationales.d: Teres minor is not the superior/anterior border; subscapularis forms anterior margin with supraspinatus.
